claims.event: Father of Geng Yan; studied the Laozi under Master Anqiu, was chain commandant of Shuodiao and governor of Shanggu, then made grand general and marquis of Xingyi by Guangwu.
Native of Maoling who joined Guangwu, raised the cavalry of Yuyang and Shanggu against Wang Lang, and was made lieutenant-general.
Younger brother of Geng Yan, appointed general for the pacification of the Hu; defeated Zhang Ye and the Wuxiao bands.
Han ruler under whom Geng Yan’s forebears held two-thousand-dan posts.
Usurper who appointed Geng Kuang; his fall brought the Gengshi Emperor to power.
Cousin of Wang Mang who studied the Laozi with Geng Kuang under Master Anqiu.
Teacher under whom Geng Kuang and Wang Ji studied the Laozi.
Ruler to whose court Geng Yan set out with tribute; summoned Zhao Yong.
Pretender who rose at Handan claiming to be Liu Ziyu, son of Emperor Cheng; Geng Yan helped defeat him.
Han ruler whose son Liu Ziyu Wang Lang pretended to be.
Clerk of Geng Yan who urged joining Wang Lang and deserted to him.
Clerk of Geng Yan who urged joining Wang Lang and deserted to him.
Founder who kept Geng Yan as a clerk, called him his host on the northern road, and made the northern commanders lieutenant-generals.
Protector of the army whom Geng Yan persuaded to let him raise troops.
Governor of Yuyang, a townsman of Guangwu, who joined in sending cavalry south.
Sent by Geng Kuang to treat with Peng Chong; marched south with Geng Yan.
Marched south with Geng Yan and Kou Xun against Wang Lang.
Governor of Dai who on Geng Kuang’s advice reported to Guangwu and was restored to his commandery.
Magistrate of Dai who rebelled with Xiongnu and Wuhuan help and was crushed by Geng Shu.

label.en: General for the Pacification of the Hu

claims.event: Enfeoffed Prince of Xiao by the Gengshi court; on Geng Yan’s advice refused to disband and made him grand general.
Ruler (Liu Xuan) whose court grew suspicious of Guangwu and sent governors north; Geng Yan described his regime as collapsing.
Appointed governor of Youzhou by the Gengshi court; put to death by Wu Han.
Gengshi appointee as governor of Shanggu, seized and executed by Geng Yan.
Gengshi appointee as governor of Yuyang, seized and executed by Geng Yan.
Urged Guangwu to defy the Gengshi court, levied Youzhou’s troops, led the vanguard cavalry, and defeated Yan Cen at Rang.
Former ruler whose day the common people looked back to, according to Geng Yan.
Sent north with Geng Yan to levy Youzhou; killed Miao Zeng; one of the thirteen generals in pursuit.
One of the thirteen generals; as general-in-chief who gallops as if flying he attacked the Yanxin bandits with Geng Yan.
One of the thirteen generals sent in pursuit east of Lu.
One of the thirteen generals sent in pursuit east of Lu.
One of the thirteen generals sent in pursuit east of Lu.

One of the thirteen generals sent in pursuit east of Lu.
One of the thirteen generals; as general of strong crossbows attacked the Yanxin bandits at Aocang.
One of the thirteen generals sent in pursuit east of Lu.
Marched out through Wuguan against Nanyang, was routed by Geng Yan at Rang and fled to Dongyang.
Man of Rang who joined Yan Cen and then surrendered.

label.en: General-in-Chief Who Gallops as if Flying

claims.event: Father of Geng Yan; sent Geng Guo to court as hostage, was advanced to marquis of Yumi, took Jundu with Geng Shu, and was summoned to the capital after Peng Chong’s death.
Volunteered to subdue Yuyang and Qi; crushed the Fuping and Huosuo bands, killed Fei Yi at Julü, and took Linzi in half a day.
Brother of Geng Yan who broke Peng Chun’s Xiongnu cavalry at Jundu and was enfeoffed marquis of Mouping.
Younger brother of Geng Shu sent by Geng Kuang to court as a hostage.
Rebel at Yuyang whom Geng Yan offered to subdue; attacked Ji Zun and Liu Xi, was driven back, and died in the fifth year.
Rebel in Zhuo whom Geng Yan proposed to seize.
Warlord of Qi based at Ju whose generals Fei Yi and Zhang Lan resisted Geng Yan.
Han Loyalty General who camped in Zhuo with Geng Yan and attacked the bandits west of Wangdu.
Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness who attacked the Wangdu and Gu’an mountain bandits with Geng Yan.
Campaign general holding Liangxiang against Peng Chong.
Valiant cavalry general holding Yangxiang against Peng Chong.
Brother of Peng Chong who led over two thousand Xiongnu horsemen against Ji Zun and Liu Xi.
Defeated the Fuping and Huosuo bandits with Geng Yan on the Pingyuan plain.
Cavalry commandant who marched east with Geng Yan against Zhang Bu.
Governor of Taishan who marched east with Geng Yan.
Zhang Bu’s grand general at Lixia, lured to relieve Julü and killed by Geng Yan.
Brother of Fei Yi who held Julü and fled to Zhang Bu.
Brother of Zhang Bu who held Xi’an and fled to Ju after Linzi fell.
Protector of the army who argued for attacking Xi’an first.
Fell ill in the twelfth year and was visited repeatedly by the emperor; posthumously titled Marquis Lie, succeeded by his youngest son Geng Ba.

Defeated Zhang Bu at Linzi and pacified Qi; in all he pacified forty-six commanderies; surrendered his grand general’s seals in the thirteenth year and died in the first year of Yongping, titled Marquis Min.
Marquis of Mouping, brother of Geng Yan, whose son Xi inherited the Mouping marquisate on his death.
Son of Geng Kuang, earlier a hostage at court, whose younger brothers Geng Guang and Geng Ju were made palace gentlemen during their father’s illness.
Younger brother of Geng Guo appointed palace gentleman during Geng Kuang’s illness.
Younger brother of Geng Guo appointed palace gentleman during Geng Kuang’s illness.
Youngest son of Geng Kuang who inherited the marquisate of Yumi; succeeded by his son Wenjin.
Son and heir of Geng Yan; as cavalry commandant fought the Xiongnu at Tianshan with distinction.
Succeeded his father Geng Zhong in Geng Yan’s marquisate and was in turn succeeded by his son Geng Liang.
Son and heir of Geng Feng, also named Wujin; married Emperor An’s sister the senior princess of Puyang and rose to palace attendant.
Succeeded his father Geng Liang, husband of the princess of Puyang, in Geng Yan’s marquisate.
Succeeded his father Marquis Ba to the marquisate of Yumi and was succeeded by his son Xi.
Succeeded his father Wenjin to the marquisate of Yumi and was succeeded by his son Xian.
Son and heir of Geng Xi; left superintendent of the Feathered Forest guard.
Son and heir of Geng Xian; married Emperor Huan’s sister the princess of Changshe and was governor of Hedong.
Grandson of Geng Yuan, the only Geng to survive Cao Cao’s purge.
Son of Geng Shu who inherited Mouping and married Emperor Ming’s daughter the princess of Longlü.
Son of Geng Xi; maternal uncle of Emperor An, made grand general; slandered the heir and Yang Zhen, was demoted by Empress Dowager Yan and killed himself.
Son of Geng Bao restored as marquis of Mouping and made palace attendant by Emperor Shun.
Nephew of Geng Bao who inherited the princess’s fief as marquis of Linlü; demoted, later exterminated by Liang Ji.
Enfeoffed marquis of Yang village in the restoration of the Geng family under Emperor Shun, alongside Geng Cheng.
Warlord who attacked Geng Yan at Linzi with two hundred thousand, was routed, fled to Pingshou and submitted.
Brother of Zhang Bu who joined the attack on Geng Yan.
Brother of Zhang Bu who joined the attack on Geng Yan.
Brother of Zhang Bu who joined the attack on Geng Yan.
Former Great Shape leader who joined Zhang Bu and met Geng Yan on the Zi River.
Engaged Zhang Bu’s vanguard before Geng Yan’s flank charge.
Advised Geng Yan to shut the camp and await the emperor.
Han founder’s general who took Lixia, compared by the emperor with Geng Yan.
Executed Li Yiji and later submitted to Gaozu.
Executed by Tian Heng, who later submitted; Gaozu forbade the commandant of the guards to avenge him.
Han founder who forbade revenge on Tian Heng.
Envoy killed by Zhang Bu; the emperor offered to have the grand minister of education set aside the feud if Zhang Bu surrendered.
Western warlord against whom Geng Yan held the line at Qi.
Palace gentleman who campaigned with Geng Yan against Anding and Beidi.
Ruler whose sister married Geng Liang; Geng Bao was his maternal uncle.
Ruler whose younger sister, the princess of Changshe, married Geng Yuan, governor of Hedong.
Later exterminated the Geng clan, leaving only Geng Yuan’s grandson Hong alive.
Ruler whose daughter married Geng Xi of Mouping.
Mother of the filial prince of Qinghe, honored as Empress Xiaode when Emperor An took the throne.
Palace attendant who with Geng Bao slandered the heir apparent.
Wet nurse of Emperor An who joined in slandering the heir apparent.
Grand Commandant ruined by Geng Bao’s faction.
Dismissed Geng Bao and Geng Cheng after Emperor An’s death.
Ruler who restored Geng Ji as marquis of Mouping.
Grand general who stripped and exterminated Geng Cheng’s household.

label.en: Left Superintendent of the Feathered Forest
Supervisor of the Left Cavalry of the Feathered Forest
Palace Gentleman of the Feathered Forest

claims.event: In the appraisal, the Marquis of Huaiyin is cited for his analysis of the Hegemon-King of Chu that foretold Gaozu’s victory.
The Hegemon-King of Chu whose position Han Xin assessed for Gaozu, as recalled in the appraisal.
In the appraisal, Gaozu’s victory is said to have been foreseen through Han Xin’s discussion of the Hegemon-King of Chu.
In the appraisal, praised for his plans in Hebei and Nanyang yet said to have won no further territory after conquering all Qi.
Appointed Geng Guo gentleman-attendant at the Yellow Gates and judged him capable; his work was foreseen through Geng Yan’s plans.
Declined to inherit his father’s marquisate in favour of his brother Ba, urged accepting Bi as southern chanyu, became grand minister of agriculture and died in office in the first year of Yongping.
On his death his son Geng Guo, next in line, yielded the succession because Geng Kuang had favoured his youngest son Ba.
Youngest son favoured by Geng Kuang, in whose favour Geng Guo declined the inheritance with imperial approval.
Xiongnu Ailizhuyu king who proclaimed himself chanyu, submitted as a vassal, and on Geng Guo’s advice was established as southern chanyu.
Cited by Geng Guo as the precedent for accepting the submission of a Xiongnu chanyu.
Grand minister of agriculture whom Geng Guo succeeded in the twenty-seventh year of Jianwu.
Later remembered Geng Guo’s counsel and instituted the general-across-the-Liao; quietly endorsed Geng Bing’s plans for a northern expedition.
Son of Geng Guo who took Jushi with Dou Gu, served as deputy to Dou Xian against the northern Xiongnu, was enfeoffed marquis of Meiyang and was mourned by the Xiongnu at his death.
Younger son of Geng Guo and brother of Geng Bing, introduced at the close of the biography.
Cavalry commandant who served as Geng Bing’s deputy against the northern Xiongnu in the sixteenth year of Yongping.
Coach commandant and imperial brother-in-law who campaigned with Geng Bing against Jushi and received the rear king’s surrender.
Rear king of Jushi who submitted to Geng Bing, clinging to his horse’s hoofs after Su An’s interference.
Major under Dou Gu who tried to divert Ande’s surrender to Dou Gu.
On his accession named Geng Bing general who campaigns west and sent him to review the Liangzhou frontier.
General of chariots and cavalry whom Geng Bing served as deputy against the northern Xiongnu; his fall cost Geng Bing’s heirs their marquisate.
Superintendent of the imperial household whom Geng Bing succeeded in the second year of Yongyuan.
Eldest son of Geng Bing who inherited the marquisate, lost it after Dou Xian’s fall, and became governor of Hanyang.
Great-grandson of Geng Bing, made minister of the lesser treasury by Cao Cao, who plotted with Ji Ping and Wei Huang to kill Cao Cao in Jian’an 23 and was exterminated with his clans.
Esteemed and promoted Geng Ji, who later plotted to kill him for planning to usurp the Han.
Grand physician-in-chief who joined Geng Ji’s failed plot against Cao Cao in Jian’an 23.
Chancellor’s upright investigator who joined Geng Ji’s failed plot against Cao Cao in Jian’an 23.

label.en: Palace Gentleman of the Five Offices

claims.event: Struck the northern chanyu’s court at Mount Jinyi with eight hundred horsemen and was made marquis of Suyi; later fought the rebel southern chanyu Tan, was flogged in prison, and twice served as general-across-the-Liao.
Chariots-and-cavalry general under whom Geng Kui served against the Xiongnu; his fall cost Geng Kui his office and title.
Left Luli king and younger brother of the northern chanyu who proclaimed himself chanyu at the Pu Sea and sought Han protection, which Geng Kui was sent to provide.
Southern chanyu whose rebellion in the third year of Yongchu Geng Kui and He Xi were sent to suppress.
Chariots-and-cavalry general who made Geng Kui his vanguard against the southern chanyu Tan.
Major sent by He Xi with Liu Zhi and two thousand men to advance with Geng Kui.
Major sent by He Xi with Geng Pu and two thousand men to advance with Geng Kui.
Palace gentleman envoy to the Xiongnu repeatedly browbeaten by Geng Kui.
Governor of Yunzhong killed by the Xianbei during the Jianguang era.
Wuhuan colonel besieged by the Xianbei at Ma city and relieved by Geng Kui and Pang Can.
Inspector of Youzhou who with Geng Kui relieved Xu Chang and drove the Xianbei beyond the passes.
Son of Geng Guang who as colonel of Wu and Ji held Jinfu and then Shule against the Xiongnu, drew water from a dry well, and killed the chanyu’s envoy rather than surrender.
Father of Geng Kui and elder brother of Geng Guang, father of Geng Gong.
Younger brother of Geng Guo and father of Geng Gong, who was orphaned young.
Cavalry commandant who campaigned against Jushi in Yongping 17 and asked for Geng Gong as his major.
Coach commandant who with Geng Gong and Geng Bing received the surrender of Jushi.
Coach commandant and cousin of Geng Gong who joined the conquest of Jushi.
Herald named colonel of Wu and Ji and stationed at Liuzhong, later besieged there by the northern Xiongnu.
Ruler under whom a princess received the board games that Wusun returned to Geng Gong.
Rear king of Jushi broken and killed by the Xiongnu before they attacked Jinfu.
The Second Division general who, as Geng Gong recalled, stabbed a mountain with his sword and made a spring gush out.
Protector-general destroyed by Yanqi and Qiuci while Geng Gong was besieged.
Died while Geng Gong was besieged, so no relief army reached him.

label.en: Left Colonel to the Grand General
Palace Gentleman Envoy to the Xiongnu

claims.event: Colonel of Wu and Ji whose memorial begging relief prompted the court debate; he died before the relief force arrived.
Newly enthroned, he convened the high ministers on Guan Chong’s plea and accepted Bao Yu’s advice to send relief.
Minister of Works who argued against sending relief to the besieged garrisons in the Western Regions.
Minister over the masses who persuaded Emperor Zhang to relieve the garrisons and later said Geng Gong’s steadfastness surpassed Su Wu’s.
Sent as general who campaigns west to garrison Jiuquan and act as its governor during the relief of the Western Regions garrisons.
Led more than seven thousand men to Liuzhong in Jianchu 1, attacked Jiaohe and forced Jushi to submit again.
Herald on the Jushi relief expedition who wished to turn back on hearing of Guan Chong’s death, but detached troops with Fan Qiang to rescue Geng Gong.
Joined Qin Peng and Wang Meng in raising troops from Zhangye, Jiuquan, Dunhuang and Shanshan for the relief of Jushi.

Rescued from Shule with only thirteen survivors reaching the Jade Gate; made cavalry commandant and colonel of the Long River, he served under Ma Fang against the Qiang but was imprisoned after Li Tan’s accusation and died at home.
Army clerk of Geng Gong who led two thousand men through deep snow to rescue the Shule garrison and was later made assistant of Gong county.
Palace gentleman who received Geng Gong’s survivors at the Jade Gate and memorialized for his enfeoffment.
Envoy held among the Xiongnu, with whom Bao Yu and the appraiser compared Geng Gong’s steadfastness.
Geng Gong’s major, rewarded after the Shule siege with the post of assistant of the Luoyang market.
Survivor of the Shule siege appointed major of the Yong camp.
Chariots-and-cavalry general against the western Qiang with Geng Gong as deputy, offended by Geng Gong’s memorial praising Dou Gu.
The late marquis of Anfeng, whom Geng Gong cited as having won the trust of the Qiang and Hu in the west.
Grand herald and descendant of Dou Rong whom Geng Gong recommended as commissioner to pacify the Liang region.
Camp-supervising herald who accused Geng Gong of neglecting his command, leading to his imprisonment.
Son of Geng Gong, tiger-fang colonel of the capital region, killed fighting rebel Qiang at Dingxi in Yuanchu 2.
Son of Geng Pu, named gentleman-attendant by edict after his father’s death in battle.
Grandson of Geng Gong who as Wuhuan colonel routed the Xianbei and was promoted general-across-the-Liao.
Early in his reign Geng Ye was appointed Wuhuan colonel.
Master Cao, cited by the appraiser for facing down a hostage at the Ke covenant.
Cited by the appraiser for asserting his state’s majesty beyond the Yellow River.
Praised in the encomium for following Geng Yan and seeing his work crowned.
Praised in the encomium alongside Geng Kuang for following Geng Yan to success.
Praised in the encomium for long-range plans that split the northern tribes.
Praised in the encomium for tracking the raiders to their lair alone.
